name: Petrol
lede: Petrol is a dark blue-green named for the iridescent sheen of petrol on water; petrol is the British word for the fuel.

sections.title: A color from a puddle
sections.body:
The color is named for the iridescent sheen that a film of petrol makes on water, the snaky shimmer on a pool of water that the artist and filmmaker Derek Jarman describes in his book on color [1]. A British dictionary of color lists *petrol blue* as a metallic shade of blue, also called petroleum blue, and describes it as a dark bluish green [2]. Who first used the word for a color is undocumented in the books [2].

The swatch itself comes from a crowd survey: the xkcd color survey of 2010 and ColorHub's own curriculum [3]. By the ISCC-NBS system it is a moderate greenish blue, 9.1 units away [3]. Neighbors in our data are [[teal]] and [[dark-teal]], and [[peacock-blue]] has the same family of iridescent associations [3].

sections.title: The swatch is not the sheen
sections.body: A flat swatch cannot show iridescence, which is a change of color with viewing angle. The screen color is only the darkest, steadiest part of what a petrol film does [1][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Petrol is rare in painting. In our archive of 23,781 paintings it appears in 47, 0.2 per cent, and is rarer than 59 per cent of the named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 0.5 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, about 4.1 times the rate the same museums would predict [4]. Inside a painting it is most often a hidden color, a dark note beneath the obvious ones (48 per cent of 25 works measured) [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment tests [4].

Google Books counts for the word *petrol* mostly measure the fuel, not the color, so we do not read a color history from them [4].
